Copper plays an essential role in connective tissue formation, iron metabolism, hematopoiesis, and central nervous system function.

Although copper deficiency is rare, it has been reported in patients with severe malabsorption, premature infants, children recovering from severe malnutrition, and patients receiving parenteral nutrition (PN) without copper supplementation.

Manifestations of copper deficiency include pancytopenia, bone abnormalities, myocardial diseases, depigmentation of skin and hair, and neurologic abnormalities., Severe copper deficiency is associated with anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and osteoporosis.

Copper is excreted primarily by the liver into the biliary system under normal physiologic conditions.
It has conventionally been recommended to exclude copper from PN in patients with cholestasis.
However, recent studies suggest that this may lead to copper deficiency.
Supplying copper though PN and monitoring serum copper concentration is now recommended.-1 Long-term PN can result in copper deficiency.

In a retrospective study of hospitalized pediatric patients receiving PN in the United States, 71% of the patients not supplemented with copper and 50% of the patients supplemented with copper had low serum copper levels of less than 75 μg/dL. The 2005 American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN) guidelines recommend providing trace elements, including copper, from PN initiation, and the recommended intake of copper in infants is 51 - JKSHP, VOL.3 20 μg/kg/day. Likewise, the 2005 European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guidelines recommended that 20 μg/kg/day of copper be supplied to parenterally fed infants and children.
However, the revised 2018 guidelines recommend that the copper intake be increased to 40 μg/kg/ day in premature infants and 20 μg/kg/day (max. 0.5 mg/day) for term infants.

It is also recommended that plasma copper levels and ceruloplasmin be monitored in patients on long-term PN. At the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of our hospital, infants receive PN which does not contain copper in the beginning, and serum copper concentration is monitored if the PN is maintained longer than 4 weeks.
When copper is deficient, infants receive 10~20 μg/kg/day of copper as multi-trace element formulations.
Serum copper concentration is monitored on a monthly basis during PN. The amount of copper is adjusted based on the patient’s serum concentrations of copper and other trace elements.

However, there are several limitations in copper supplementation through PN. Since single-entity intravenous (IV) copper products are not available in Korea, IV copper should be supplemented with only multi-trace element products.
The composition of such products is often not suitable for infants, resulting in an unmet supply of each trace element.
Neonatal multi-trace element preparations can provide trace elements in amounts closer to the requirements in neonates.
However, other trace elements, such as manganese and chromium, make it still difficult to supply copper at the recommended doses.
Also, its expensive cost is not covered by national health insurance.
There is a lack of research on copper sup- - 45 38, NO.4 (20 plementation in long-term PN patients in Korea, especially on copper deficiency and evaluation of IV copper supplementation in infants.

This study aimed to analyze the incidence of and risk factors for copper deficiency and evaluate IV copper supplementation in infants requiring long-term PN. This research can help to prevent copper deficiency in infants.

Research subjects We included patients who were admitted to the NICU of our hospital from July of 2015 to June of 2020, had their serum copper concentration measured at least once during their hospital stay, and received PN for more than two weeks in this study.

Patients were divided into a deficient group (with a serum copper concentration of <70 μg/dL) and a non-deficient group (with a serum copper concentration of ≥70 μg/dL) based on their serum copper concentrations.
Serum copper concentration was defined as the first measured value after admission to the NICU.

This study found that the incidence of copper deficiency in infants requiring longterm PN was as high as 61.9%.
This was similar to a previous study in children receiving PN (with a copper deficiency rate of 50~71%).
However, the previous study included pediatric patients ranging from preterm infants to teenagers.
This study focused on infants.
In the group with copper deficiency, gestational age and birth weight were significantly lower and the proportion of preterm infants and extremely low birth weight infants was significantly higher.
In particular, gestational age younger than 32 weeks was an independent risk factor for copper deficiency.
Since most copper accumulation occurs during the third trimester of pregnancy, copper deficiency can be more likely in preterm infants.
The proportion of BPD patients was significantly higher in the copper deficiency group.

Copper is an important component of pulmonary superoxide dismutase, and these antioxidant enzymes can prevent lung injury 57 - JKSHP, VOL.3 caused by oxygenation therapy., In the copper deficiency group, the proportion of BPD patients may be higher due to the lack of lung injury prevention by antioxidant enzymes.
The copper-deficient group had a longer NICU stay, lower ANC and hemoglobin levels, a lower platelet count, and a higher proportion of rickets.
Symptoms of copper deficiency include pancytopenia and skeletal system abnormalities.
The patients in this study demonstrated such clinical results due to copper deficiency.
Therefore, adequate copper supplementation is required to prevent the clinical consequences of copper deficiency.

In baseline characteristics of the subjects of this study, gestational age, birth weight, and the proportion of preterm infants and extremely low birth weight infants was significantly different in both groups.
Therefore, further research is needed on the association between copper deficiency and clinical outcomes such as BPD and rickets.

Serum copper concentrations may be increased in patients with acute inflammation and may be falsely elevated when CRP is higher than 4 mg/dL.,, In this study, hs-CRP tended to be higher in the copper non-deficient group than in the deficient group, but this was not statistically significant.

Moreover, the average hs-CRP of all subjects was 1.6 mg/dL, and the average in the copper non-deficient group was 2.5 mg/ dL, which was less than 4 mg/dL. In the subgroup analysis, the average IV copper supply was 11.6±3.9 μg/kg/day. Serum copper concentration increased significantly after IV copper supplementation.

The 2005 ASPEN guidelines recommend supplying 20 μg/kg/day of copper to preterm and - 45 38, NO.4 (20 term infants and the 2018 ESPEN guidelines recommend 40 μg/kg/day in preterm infants and 20 μg/kg/day (max. 0.5 mg/day) in fullterm infants., In comparison, the copper supply in this subgroup was low. Although IV copper was administered less than the recommended dose, a significant increase in serum concentration was observed.
In preterm infants, the average serum copper level after supplementation was 67.0±18.5 μg/ dL, which was still within the range of copper deficiency.
Especially, more attention is required in premature infants with lower serum copper concentrations.
In this subgroup, especially in preterm infants, the copper supply may have been insufficient.
A higher copper supply is required based on the ASPEN and ESPEN guidelines.
However, there are several limitations in supplying copper to meet the recommended intake.
There is no single-entity IV copper product available in Korea, and the composition of multi-trace element products is often not suitable for infants.
Chromium or manganese deficiencies, which are components of multi-trace element products, are rare.
These two trace elements can accumulate in patients receiving long-term PN. Manganese accumulation, in particular, raises concerns about neurotoxicity.
Therefore, single-entity IV copper or multi-trace element products suitable for infants are needed to supply adequate copper to this population.
Since copper is excreted primarily by the liver through the biliary system, it has conventionally been recommended to exclude copper from PN in patients with cholestasis.

However, recent studies suggest that this can lead to copper deficiency, and the recommendation is now to supply copper 58 - 김유진 : 장기간 정맥 영양 의존적 신생 through PN and monitor serum copper concentrations.-1 In this study, there was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients with cholestasis in the copper-deficient and non-deficient groups.
The average copper supply in patients with and without cholestasis was 11.8 μg/kg/day and 11.2 μg/kg/day, respectively, which showed no statistically significant difference (p=0.7.
This study has the following limitations.
First, this study was a retrospective study conducted at a single institution.
Several factors, including the timing of copper measurements, were not controlled.
The proportions of clinical characteristics may have been underestimated because it was a retrospective analysis based on electronic medical records.
Secondly, many subjects were nourished with enteral nutrition and parenteral nutrition, and it was difficult to calculate the amount of copper supplied through enteral nutrition.

Among the patients included in this study, 81% had gastrointestinal surgery and 58.7% had gastrointestinal diseases, which made it difficult to estimate the amount of copper supplied through enteral nutrition.
Also, there were limitations in quantifying the amount of copper provided through enteral nutrition because the types, methods, and amounts of enteral nutrition varied among the patients.
Third, the number of subjects was insufficient, especially in the subgroup, which resulted in reduced statistical power.
It is thought that serum copper concentrations can be reduced due to insufficient body store, depletion during the period when copper is not supplied, and inadequate copper supply.

In addition, it is thought that serum copper concentrations may be decreased due - 45 생아에서의 구리 결핍 현황과 공급 평가 to insufficient absorption of copper due to the immaturity of the gastrointestinal tract, gastrointestinal diseases, and feeding intolerance.

Additional studies for optimal copper provision in infants are needed, and individualized dose adjustment is required according to the body store of copper, and the function and absorption rate of the gastrointestinal tract.
This study analyzed the incidence of and risk factors for copper deficiency and evaluated appropriate copper supplementation in infants requiring long-term PN in Korea.
The results of this study are a basis in neonatal PN consults to recommend appropriate copper supplementation considering the risk factors of copper deficiency.

In the future, a prospective study on the causal relationship between the appropriate copper dosage and clinical outcomes according to gestational age and clinical characteristics in infants on long-term PN is necessary.

Copper deficiency is common in infants receiving long-term PN without copper, especially in patients with a young gestational age. In the copper-deficient group, ANC, hemoglobin, and platelet counts were lower, and the proportion of BPD and rickets was higher.
Therefore, an adequate supply of copper is required to prevent the clinical consequences of a deficiency.
It is necessary to develop single-entity IV copper or multi-trace element products with a composition suitable for infants.
